points.title: Usefulness and reliability
points.brief: A source is reliable if it can be trusted to be accurate, and useful if it helps answer your question. Even a biased source can be useful as evidence of a point of view.

points.title: Bias and propaganda
points.brief: Bias is a one-sided view that comes from who made a source and why. Propaganda is made on purpose to persuade, often by governments in wartime.

points.title: Corroborating sources
points.brief: Historians check a source against other sources, and a claim that several independent sources support is stronger.

points.title: Historians' interpretations
points.brief: Historians interpret the same events differently because of the evidence they use, the questions they ask and the time they write in.

points.title: Building a historical argument
points.brief: A historical argument states a clear thesis, supports each point with evidence from sources and explains how the evidence proves the point.

units.title: The making of the modern world

points.title: The Industrial Revolution in brief
points.brief: From about 1750, Britain moved from making goods by hand to making them by machines in factories, and people moved to cities for work.

points.title: The American Revolution
points.brief: The American colonies broke from Britain in a war from 1775 to 1783, and their Declaration of Independence claimed rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

points.title: The French Revolution
points.brief: From 1789 the French overthrew their king and declared the rights of man and of the citizen, spreading ideas of equality, democracy and the rule of law.

points.title: Nationalism and nation-states
points.brief: Nationalism is the belief that a people sharing a language and culture should rule themselves, which led to new nation-states such as Italy and Germany in the 1800s.

points.title: Empires and the movement of peoples
points.brief: European empires moved millions of people, through the slave trade, convict transportation to Australia and migration in search of land and work.

points.title: Causes of the First World War
points.brief: Militarism, alliances, imperial rivalry and nationalism raised tensions in Europe, and the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in 1914 set off the war.

points.title: The Paris Peace Conference
points.brief: In 1919 the winners redrew the map of Europe, set up the League of Nations and made Germany accept blame and pay reparations in the Treaty of Versailles.

points.title: Extremism between the wars
points.brief: Anger at the peace treaties and the Great Depression helped extreme movements gain power, such as fascism in Italy, Nazism in Germany and communism in the Soviet Union.

points.title: Democracy in the colonies
points.brief: In the 1850s Australian colonies gained their own parliaments, and they were among the first places to use the secret ballot and give most men the vote.

points.title: The road to Federation
points.brief: Supporters such as Henry Parkes argued for defence, free trade between colonies and a national identity, others had doubts, and voters approved the Constitution before the colonies federated on 1 January 1901.

points.title: Australia's system of government
points.brief: Federation split power between the Commonwealth and the states, set out in the Constitution, with a parliament, government and courts, and NSW kept its own parliament for state matters.

points.title: The White Australia policy
points.brief: The Immigration Restriction Act 1901 used a dictation test to keep out people who were not white, and it shaped migration for decades.

points.title: Workers' rights
points.brief: Trade unions and the Labor Party pushed for workers' rights, and the Harvester judgment of 1907 set a basic wage to support a family.

points.title: Votes for women
points.brief: The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 gave most women the right to vote and stand in federal elections, but left out most Aboriginal people and many people of Asian and Pacific background.

chapters.title: Australia in the First World War

points.title: Why Australia went to war
points.brief: As part of the British Empire, Australia joined the war in 1914, and many men enlisted out of loyalty to Britain, adventure or pay.

points.title: Gallipoli
points.brief: On 25 April 1915 Australian and New Zealand troops landed at Gallipoli in Turkey, and after eight months and heavy losses they withdrew.

points.title: The Western Front
points.brief: Most Australians fought in France and Belgium, in trench battles such as Fromelles and Pozières in 1916, where casualties were very high.

points.title: The War Precautions Act and the home front
points.brief: The War Precautions Act 1914 let the government censor news, control the economy and intern people of German background, while women and others raised money and supplies.

points.title: The conscription votes
points.brief: Australians voted twice, in 1916 and 1917, on whether men could be forced to fight overseas, bitterly divided debates that ended in No both times.

points.title: The impact of the war on different groups
points.brief: The war affected groups differently, such as Aboriginal soldiers who served but were not treated as equals on return, migrants under suspicion and women taking new roles.

points.title: The Anzac legend
points.brief: The Anzac legend describes soldiers as brave, loyal to their mates and tough. It is remembered on Anzac Day, and historians debate whose stories it leaves out.

points.title: Causes of the Second World War
points.brief: Long-term causes included the Treaty of Versailles and the Great Depression, and short-term causes included Hitler's expansion and Germany's invasion of Poland in 1939.

points.title: Australia enters the war
points.brief: Prime Minister Menzies announced in September 1939 that Australia was at war because Britain was, and people enlisted for many reasons.

points.title: North Africa and Crete
points.brief: Australians fought in North Africa, including the siege of Tobruk in 1941, and in the failed defence of Greece and Crete that same year.

points.title: The fall of Singapore
points.brief: Japan captured Singapore in February 1942, and about 15,000 Australians became prisoners of war, a shock that showed Britain could not defend Australia.

points.title: The Battle for Australia
points.brief: In 1942 Japan bombed Darwin and Australians fought on the Kokoda Track in New Guinea, and Australia turned to the United States for help in the Pacific War.

points.title: Government controls
points.brief: The government rationed food and clothing, censored the news and directed people into war work to support the war effort.

points.title: Women's changing roles in WWII
points.brief: Women joined the services and took jobs in factories and on farms that men had done, though usually for lower pay.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander service in WWII
points.brief: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people served in the forces, including the Torres Strait Light Infantry Battalion, and worked as scouts, labourers and coast watchers.

points.title: Internment of enemy aliens
points.brief: People in Australia of German, Italian and Japanese background were seen as enemy aliens, and thousands were held in internment camps.

points.title: Prisoners of war
points.brief: Australians held by Japan, such as at Changi and on the Burma-Thailand Railway, faced starvation, disease and forced labour, and many died.

points.title: The Holocaust
points.brief: Nazi Germany murdered about six million Jewish people, along with Roma, disabled people and others, and some survivors later rebuilt their lives in Australia.

points.title: Coming home from war
points.brief: Returning personnel faced injuries and lasting trauma, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander veterans were often left out of help such as land for soldier settlers.

points.title: The Nuremberg trials and the Genocide Convention
points.brief: The Nuremberg trials from 1945 put Nazi leaders on trial for war crimes, and in 1948 the United Nations agreed the Genocide Convention to prevent and punish genocide.

units.title: The modern world and human rights

points.title: The United Nations
points.brief: The United Nations was formed in 1945 to keep peace and promote cooperation, with a General Assembly of all members and a Security Council.

points.title: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights
points.brief: In 1948 the UN agreed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, listing rights for everyone, and Australia's H. V. Evatt was President of the General Assembly when it passed.

points.title: The Cold War
points.brief: After 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union competed for power without fighting each other directly, and fear of nuclear war shaped films, music and daily life.

points.title: New technologies after 1945
points.brief: Television, computers, jet travel and later the internet changed how people worked, communicated and spent their free time.

points.title: Environmental awareness
points.brief: From the 1960s people grew concerned about pollution and damage to nature, which led to environmental movements and laws.

points.title: Early Aboriginal activism
points.brief: Aboriginal activists such as William Cooper, Jack Patten and William Ferguson held a Day of Mourning on 26 January 1938 to demand equal rights.

points.title: The US civil rights movement
points.brief: African Americans, led by people such as Martin Luther King Jr, used protests and boycotts to end segregation, which inspired activists in Australia.

points.title: The 1965 Freedom Ride
points.brief: Charles Perkins and members of Student Action for Aborigines rode a bus through towns such as Walgett and Moree to expose racial segregation in NSW.

points.title: The 1967 Referendum
points.brief: Over 90 per cent of voters agreed to let the Commonwealth make laws for Aboriginal people and to count them in the census, a strong sign of support for change.

points.title: The Stolen Generations
points.brief: Government policies removed many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families, and the Bringing Them Home report of 1997 told their stories.

points.title: The Wave Hill walk-off
points.brief: In 1966 Gurindji workers led by Vincent Lingiari walked off Wave Hill station over pay and conditions, and the strike became a fight for their land.

points.title: The Aboriginal Tent Embassy
points.brief: In 1972 activists set up a tent embassy outside Parliament House in Canberra to demand land rights, a protest that continues.

points.title: Land rights laws
points.brief: The Aboriginal Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976 and the NSW Aboriginal Land Rights Act 1983 let Aboriginal people claim back some land.

points.title: Mabo and native title
points.brief: In 1992 the High Court's Mabo decision, won by Eddie Mabo for the Meriam people, rejected terra nullius, and the Native Title Act 1993 followed.

points.title: Reclaiming languages and cultures
points.brief: Aboriginal communities are reviving languages and cultural practices that colonisation suppressed, which strengthens identity and connection to Country.

points.title: The women's movement in Australia
points.brief: Women campaigned for equal pay, won in decisions of 1969 and 1972, for an end to the ban on married women in public service jobs and for the Sex Discrimination Act 1984.

points.title: Human rights conventions
points.brief: International agreements, such as conventions on racial discrimination and the rights of the child, set standards that countries like Australia agree to and that shape their laws.

points.title: Closing the Gap
points.brief: Gaps between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal Australians in health, education and life expectancy remain, and Closing the Gap, begun in 2008, sets targets to reduce them.

points.title: The Agricultural Revolution
points.brief: New farming methods and the enclosure of common land produced more food with fewer workers, so many people left villages for towns.

points.title: Steam power and new inventions
points.brief: The steam engine, spinning and weaving machines and railways changed how goods were made and moved.

points.title: Factories, mines and child labour
points.brief: Workers, including young children, worked long hours in dangerous factories and mines for low pay.

points.title: Reform movements
points.brief: Reformers, trade unions and the Chartists pushed for change, and Factory Acts began to limit children's working hours.

points.title: Industrial cities and their legacy
points.brief: Industry made Britain powerful and its cities grew fast, crowded and polluted, and the changes spread around the world.

points.title: Populate or perish
points.brief: In 1945 Australia had about 7 million people, mostly of British background, and the government set out to grow the population for defence and industry.

points.title: Post-war migrants
points.brief: After WWII displaced people and migrants from Britain and Europe came to Australia, many working on projects such as the Snowy Mountains Scheme.

points.title: The end of the White Australia policy
points.brief: The White Australia policy was eased from 1966 and ended by the Whitlam government in 1973, opening migration to people from Asia and elsewhere.

points.title: Multiculturalism
points.brief: In the 1970s the Whitlam and Fraser governments made multiculturalism official policy, supporting migrants to keep their cultures and languages.

points.title: Refugees from Vietnam
points.brief: After the Vietnam War ended in 1975, many Vietnamese refugees fled by boat or through camps, and tens of thousands resettled in Australia.

points.title: How migration changed Australia
points.brief: Migrants changed Australia's population, economy, food and culture, and strengthened links with their countries of origin.
